domain: Medieval Political Economy / Legal History / Institutional Analysis
topic_summary: Analysis of the codification of feudal obligations in medieval Europe, focusing on the structural contest between lords and vassals over the interpretation of reciprocal oaths. The shared commitment to codified feudal relationships instantiated radically different constraints depending on whether the kernel was read as authorizing maximal extraction or as establishing bounded, conditional coordination.

key_entities: Vassals (subordinates claiming protection of bounded obligations)
Royal Courts (emerging state authority claiming interpretation monopoly)
Written Charters (codification artifacts with contested interpretation)
key_tensions: Extraction maximization vs obligation boundedness (lords vs vassals on same kernel)
Written codification vs customary flexibility (formalization creates new interpretive authority)
key_mechanisms: Oath ceremonies (ritual binding creating shared commitment substrate)
Charter drafting (codification process where ambiguity is strategically preserved or eliminated)
Ecclesiastical adjudication (Church courts interpreting feudal disputes pre-royal court monopoly)
key_absences: Peasant interpretation (third reading of same kernel from below feudal contract)
Transition mechanism from customary to codified (how codification process itself altered the constraint)

axes.structural_delta: Feudal oath read as strictly bounded reciprocal contract: military service for protection, with fixed limits on taxation and labor
axes.primary_observable: Vassal resistance patterns; charter clauses limiting lordly exactions; frequency of appeal to external adjudicators
axes.selection_reason: Second reading of contested kernel; structurally opposed victim set and ε to lord reading

axes.selection_reason: Third reading from external interpretive authority; captures inter-institutional contest dimension

Peasant reading deferred but may be the true extraction ceiling. If so, lord-vassal contest is distributive fight over a fixed surplus, not a kernel contest over constraint structure.

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: Reciprocal feudal oath: lord provides military protection and land tenure, vassal provides military service and loyalty. Codified in charters with deliberately ambiguous extraction limits.
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Interpretive legitimacy contested: lords claim customary right to define obligations, vassals claim charter text limits extraction, church claims canon law supremacy over secular oaths.
commitment_system_recognition.candidate_pattern: Deferred Maintenance (drift absorbed through charter reinterpretation without formal revision)

readings.commitment: Feudal oath authorizes maximal extraction bounded only by vassal service capacity
readings.expected_structural_delta: High ε snare: vassals in victim set, extraction limited only by rebellion threshold

readings.commitment: Feudal oath establishes fixed, bounded reciprocal obligations enforced by charter text
readings.authority_grounding: Written charter / appeal to external adjudicators
readings.expected_structural_delta: Low ε rope: coordination mechanism with mutual enforceability, no structural victim

readings.commitment: Feudal oath bound by Christian charity and sacramental oath obligations, limiting secular extraction
readings.authority_grounding: Canon law / church courts / threat of excommunication
readings.expected_structural_delta: Moderate ε tangled_rope: church gains interpretive authority, lords constrained by theological limits

axiom_contradictions.basis: Lord reading treats oath as unilateral授权 (authorization) for extraction; vassal reading treats oath as bilateral contract with enforceable limits. No single framework holds both 'lord has unilateral right to define obligations' and 'obligations are fixed by mutual agreement.' These are axiomatically incompatible accounts of contractual authority.

Lord reading grounds authority in secular customary prerogative; church reading subordinates secular authority to divine law enforced by ecclesiastical courts. No single framework holds both 'secular lord is final authority on oath interpretation' and 'divine law constrains secular authority through church adjudication.' These are incompatible sovereignty claims.
